case.question: what is the difference between ron and mon
case.expected_answer: MON uses more demanding test conditions than RON: 900 rather than 600 rpm, a preheated fuel mixture and variable ignition timing. For modern pump gasoline, MON is typically about 8–12 points lower, depending on fuel composition; there is no fixed conversion.
case.support_quote: Another type of octane rating, called Motor Octane Number (MON), is determined at 900 rpm engine speed instead of the 600 rpm for RON.[1] MON testing uses a similar test engine to that used in RON testing, but with a preheated fuel mixture, higher engine speed, and variable ignition timing to further stress the fuel's knock resistance. Depending on the composition of the fuel, the MON of a modern pump gasoline will be about 8 to 12 octane lower than the RON, but there is no direct link between RON and MON.
case.source_qualification: The approximate 8–12-point difference applies to modern pump gasoline in this reference and depends on fuel composition.
family_reference_texts: Another type of octane rating, called Motor Octane Number (MON), is determined at 900 rpm engine speed instead of the 600 rpm for RON.[1] MON testing uses a similar test engine to that used in RON testing, but with a preheated fuel mixture, higher engine speed, and variable ignition timing to further stress the fuel's knock resistance. Depending on the composition of the fuel, the MON of a modern pump gasoline will be about 8 to 12 octane lower than the RON, but there is no direct link between RON and MON. Pump gasoline specifications typically require both a minimum RON and a minimum MON.[citation needed]
